Limitation
- I can’t access or modify your attached spreadsheet in this session because no spreadsheet tool/connector is available and you haven’t pasted any rows. I cannot inspect the workbook, detect which columns contain formulas, or make changes.

Concrete next step (pick one)
1) Ask me to do the work: attach the workbook here (or enable a spreadsheet tool) so I can inspect it and run the cleaning steps. If you attach it, tell me which column(s) define a “duplicate” (e.g., CustomerID, Email) and which sheet to operate on. I will then (a) preview the changes, (b) run the cleaning while keeping formulas intact, and (c) show exactly what I will change before you accept anything.

2) Do it yourself (recommended, preserves formulas): use Power Query in Excel to clean duplicates and fix dates without altering formulas in the original sheet:
   - Make a backup copy of the workbook first.
   - Select your data table (or convert the range to a table: Home > Format as Table) and choose Data > From Table/Range (this opens Power Query).
   - In Power Query:
     - Remove duplicates: select the key column(s) (e.g., CustomerID, Email) → Home > Remove Rows > Remove Duplicates.
     - Fix broken date formats: select the date column → Transform > Data Type > Using Locale… → choose Date and the locale that matches how the dates were entered (this parses many odd formats). If needed, use Transform > Replace Values or add a custom column using Date.FromText with a culture.
   - Close & Load To… and load the cleaned table to a new sheet (don’t overwrite the sheet that contains formulas). This produces a cleaned copy so your original formulas remain untouched.
   - If you need the cleaned data to replace the original, verify formula references first, then replace the data (or update formulas to reference the new sheet).

Quick alternative (if Power Query unavailable)
- Make a full-sheet copy (right-click sheet → Move or Copy → Create a copy).
- On the copy, Data > Remove Duplicates (choose key columns).
- For date column issues: try Data > Text to Columns (Delimited → Finish) then format the column as Date, or use a formula in a helper column to normalize strings to parseable date values (e.g., DATEVALUE or DATE/MID/LEFT/RIGHT parsing) and copy results as values.

If you want, upload the workbook (or paste 10–20 representative rows including headers) and I’ll give the specific Power Query steps or formulas tailored to your columns.
